entries.content: V*/W = variable capital / total employee compensation. Under the approximation ec_u/ec_p ≈ 1 (where ec is employee compensation per worker), V*/W ≈ Lp/L. This approximation is central to the extension methodology: V*/W is proxied by the productive labor share.
Book benchmarks from Table 5.7: 1948=0.54, 1967=0.45, 1989=0.36. These track close to but slightly below Lp/L values, confirming the ec_u/ec_p ≈ 1 approximation (it is actually slightly > 1).
Fig 9.3 uses V*/W in the profit rate decomposition, showing how the productive wage share mediates between the exploitation rate and the overall profit rate.

The V*/W ≈ Lp/L approximation holds when unproductive and productive workers earn similar per-capita compensation. Empirically, V*/W is slightly below Lp/L (0.54 vs 0.57 in 1948; 0.36 vs 0.36 in 1989), suggesting ec_u/ec_p has converged toward 1 over time.

Mohun's unproductive decomposition data (mohun_unproductive_decomposition*.csv) allows computing alternative V*/W estimates under his broader productive classification. His productive sector includes Information and retail eating/drinking.

V*/W is the key input to S504 (V*) and S506 (e) extensions. Any error in V*/W propagates multiplicatively through the entire distributional analysis. Post-1989 wage inequality trends may cause ec_u/ec_p to diverge from 1.

[internal-decision-record]: BLS CES production/nonsupervisory worker ratios are used as the proxy for IO-based productive/unproductive labor decomposition when extending S512. S512 extension is certified at 76% faithfulness (CERTIFIED WITH NOTES). Cross-validated against Mohun (2005) estimates.
V_j ≡ ec_j · (Lp)_j ≡ (Wp)_j = variable capital in the jth production sector; V* ≡ Wp = ∑ (Wp)_j = total variable capital.
entries.context: Section 5.3, p. 113: definition of V* whose ratio to W gives S512. Wp/W = V*/W is the operational quantity S512 reports.

entries.content: Figures 5.10 and 5.11 make quite explicit that the unit wages of productive and unproductive workers change only slightly, whereas their relative employments change drastically. We can therefore unambiguously conclude that the relative decline in productive to total wages Wp/W (= V*/W) is almost entirely due to the relative decline in productive to total employment Lp/L.
entries.context: Section 5.3, p. 113: empirical equivalence V*/W ≈ Lp/L under ec_u/ec_p ≈ 1. Direct warrant for the ec_u/ec_p ≈ 1 approximation used in S512.

entries.content: At the beginning of the postwar period the wage of unproductive workers is some 11%-12% higher than that of productive workers, but this relative advantage gradually disappears until, by the end of the period, unproductive wages are 3%-4% lower than productive wages.
entries.context: Section 5.6, p. 130: documents the slow convergence of ec_p and ec_u over 1948-1989, supporting the approximation that V*/W tracks Lp/L within a small drift.

Table 5.14, p. 140 (extracted_content/tables/page_140_marxian_orthodox_comparison.csv): the typical relative level of V*/W at the 1967 midperiod is 42% and the change over 1948-89 is -33%. **DRIFT FLAG**: registry currently lists 1967=0.45 — book reference is 0.42. The -33% change anchors 1948 at ~0.54 and 1989 at ~0.36, exactly matching Table 5.7 endpoints (0.54, 0.36). Also consistent with chunk_14 p.113: 'V*/W declines by 34%'. The 11%-12% wage-advantage at 1948 narrowing to -3%-4% by 1989 (p.130) explains why V*/W < Lp/L early and V*/W ≈ Lp/L late.

entries.content: Figure 5.8 contrasts the levels of real variable capital and of the total real wage bill. Their absolute growth is greater than that of the corresponding labor totals in Figure 5.7 because the wage measures also incorporate the effects of growing real wages. But the relative movements of wage and employment measures is virtually the same, as is evident in Figure 5.9. V*/W declines by 34%, while Lp/L declines by 37%.
entries.context: Section 5.3, p. 113 (HDARP chunk_14): the book's explicit numerical trend statement for V*/W: a 34% decline 1948-89 (Figure 5.9). Combined with Table 5.14's -33% change and 1967 midpoint of 42%, this gives a fully redundant anchor for S512's reference trajectory: 0.54 (1948) → 0.42 (1967) → 0.36 (1989).

citations.full: Shaikh, Anwar, and E. Ahmet Tonak. 1994. Measuring the Wealth of Nations: The Political Economy of National Accounts. Cambridge University Press.
Mohun, Simon. 2013. 'Unproductive Labor in the U.S. Economy 1964-2010.' Review of Radical Political Economics 46(3): 355-379.

methodology_summary: Productive wage share V*/W ≈ Lp/L under the ec_u/ec_p ≈ 1 approximation. Book benchmarks decline from 0.54 (1948) to 0.36 (1989). Critical input to S504 and S506 extensions. Extended via BLS CES proxy ([internal-decision-record], faithfulness 76%).
known_issues: ec_u/ec_p ≈ 1 may deteriorate with rising wage inequality post-1989
Error propagates multiplicatively to S504 and S506
